newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Unite to win, UK minister tells Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Unite to win, UK minister tells Conservatives.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservative Party can claw back its huge opinion poll deficit and win the coming general election if it closes ranks over Europe, Trade Secretary Ian Lang said on Wednesday.

Lang, a close colleague of Prime Minister John Major, dismissed opinion polls as "a bit of media fun" and predicted that the Conservatives would come from behind and win, just as they did against the odds at the 1992 general election.
"Five years ago we were deeply unpopular in the opinion polls but we won that election. Five years ago we were divided over Europe but we came together and we won that election.
"I believe we can do the same this time," Lang, who is attending the inaugural ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation, told Reuters.

But Lang said victory depended on Conservative "Euro-sceptics" calling off the fierce guerrilla war they have waged against Major over his refusal to rule out Britain's participation in the European Union's planned single currency.
"The party must come together. We can only win if we remain united," Lang said.

Major, who must hold an election by May 22, made a passionate appeal for unity at the weekend only to hear Euro-sceptic legislator Teresa Gorman call the next day for a referendum on Britain's membership of the EU.

In a warning to the Euro-sceptics, who are deeply hostile to closer European integration, Lang said only Major's wait-and-see stance on the single currency could both defend Britain's interests and unite the ruling party.

"I believe that after the recent spat the time has come to settle down and stand behind the position," he said. "It's important that we do put our differences behind us and that we concentrate our fire on our political opponents."
Major lost his majority in the 651-seat House of Commons last week when a Conservative member of parliament withdrew his support in protest over local hospital cuts.

Lang said the Conservatives, in power since 1979 but more than 20 points behind the main opposition Labour party, needed to concentrate on getting across the message of the government's success in reviving Britain's economy.
"We have fundamental economic strength now such as we've not had in my lifetime," the minister said.

Lang said a swing to the Conservatives in elections for local councils showed that the government's record of falling unemployment, low inflation and rising living standards was getting through to voters.

"We've got to sustain the policies that have created that situation. That does mean another Conservative government. I think the people of Britain are more and more beginning to recognise that," he added.
